_about: Visual ('See') content. Original diagrams and charts drawn by the app from syllabus content; numbers are computed by calc.js from the worked example named in `source`. Every item has a text `description` (shown under 'Text description') and charts also get a data table. place = 'learn' (default) shows it on the Learn page; items with `example` appear under that example in Practise.

items.title: Up 10%, then down 10%
items.description: Three bars: the share starts at 100, rises to 110 after a 10% gain, then falls to 99 after a 10% loss, because the fall is applied to the bigger base of 110.

items.title: Five monthly returns and their mean
items.description: Monthly returns of 2%, −1%, 3%, 0% and 1%, with their mean of 1%. The sample standard deviation, a measure of how spread out they are around the mean, is 1.58%.

items.title: The map of markets
items.description: Five ways to divide the financial markets: money versus capital markets (under one year versus longer); debt versus equity; primary (new issues) versus secondary (resale); exchange-traded versus over-the-counter; and spot (cash) versus derivatives markets.

items.title: One saver, one power station

nodes.label: 10-year bond
nodes.sub: a promise to pay interest and repay

items.description: Money flows from a teacher in Nairobi, through contributions to a pension fund, which buys a 10-year bond issued by an electricity utility; the utility uses the money to build a solar plant. Promises flow back the other way: the bond promises interest and repayment to the fund, which pays the teacher’s pension.

items.title: World equity and bond markets, end of 2025 (US$ trillion)
items.description: Global equity market capitalisation was about US$157.8 trillion, of which the US was 43.7% (about 69.0) and the rest of the world about 88.8. Global bonds outstanding were about US$160.7 trillion, of which the US was 38.1% (about 61.2) and the rest of the world about 99.5. Figures from SIFMA’s 2026 Capital Markets Fact Book [R1].

items.title: Who touches a trade? (South Africa)
items.description: A pension fund’s asset manager decides to buy JSE-listed shares. The order goes to a broker that is a JSE member, is executed on the JSE trading system, is cleared, and settles through Strate, South Africa’s central securities depository, into the fund’s custodian.

items.title: The careers map
items.description: Front-office roles generate revenue: sales, trading, origination and portfolio management. Middle-office roles control risk: risk, compliance and product control. Back-office roles process trades: operations and settlements. Technology, data and quantitative roles support all three.

items.title: From news to prices
items.description: A chain of likely reactions: inflation published well above expectations leads markets to expect a higher (or not lower) policy rate; government bond yields rise and bond prices fall; the currency may strengthen as higher rates attract foreign money; share prices may fall as future profits are discounted at higher rates.

items.title: Real return on a 10% deposit as inflation changes
items.description: The real return on a deposit paying 10% falls as inflation rises, crossing zero when inflation reaches 10%. At 5% inflation the exact real return is 4.76%.

items.title: R10,000 growing at 8% a year
items.description: R10,000 compounding at 8% a year reaches R14,693.28 after 5 years and roughly doubles after about 9 years (72 / 8). The curve bends upwards because interest is earned on earlier interest.

items.title: The project’s cash flows
items.description: A cost of 10,000 today (a negative bar) followed by inflows of 3,000, 4,000 and 5,000 at the end of years 1 to 3. Discounted at 10% the NPV is −210.37; the IRR is 8.90%.

items.title: NPV profile of the project
items.description: NPV falls as the discount rate rises. It is +2,000 at 0%, crosses zero at the IRR of about 8.90%, and is −210.37 at the 10% hurdle rate, so the project is rejected at 10%.

items.title: A repo: two legs

nodes.label: Day 0
nodes.sub: Bank sells bonds worth 10,200,000 to a fund for 10,000,000 cash

nodes.label: Days 1–7
nodes.sub: The fund holds the bonds as collateral (haircut 1.96%)

nodes.label: Day 7
nodes.sub: Bank buys the bonds back for 10,013,424.66 (7% repo rate)

items.description: In the first leg the bank sells government bonds worth 10,200,000 to a fund for 10,000,000 in cash. In the second leg, 7 days later, it buys them back for 10,013,424.66, which includes 13,424.66 of interest at 7%. Economically it is a secured loan; the 1.96% haircut protects the fund.

items.title: One Treasury bill quoted three ways
items.description: The same 91-day bill is quoted at a 4.00% discount yield, a 4.04% money-market yield and a 4.10% bond-equivalent yield. Always compare like with like.

items.title: Bond structures

groups.title: How the coupon works
items: Floating-rate notes (reset to a reference rate)

groups.title: Other
items: Labelled: green, social, sustainability, sustainability-linked, blue

items.description: Bonds differ in how the coupon works (fixed, zero-coupon, floating-rate, inflation-linked), in embedded options (callable, putable, convertible), in whether they are backed by assets (asset-backed, mortgage-backed, covered bonds), and in other forms: hybrid and perpetual bonds, sukuk, and labelled bonds such as green, social, sustainability, sustainability-linked and blue bonds.

items.title: Coupon rate versus current yield
items.description: A 6% coupon bond trading at 95 has a current yield of 6.32%, above its coupon, because it trades below face value.

items.title: One day, three index returns
items.description: With the same share prices, a price-weighted index rises 5.29% (the high-priced share A dominates), a market-cap-weighted index falls 1.43% (the largest company, B, dominates) and an equal-weighted index rises 1.67%.

items.title: Rights issue: before and after
items.description: Before the issue the share is 50. New shares are offered at 40, one for every four held. The theoretical ex-rights price is 48 and each right is worth 8.

items.title: Reading a quote: USD/ZAR 17.9950 / 18.0050

groups.title: USD
items: Base currency: one dollar is being priced

groups.title: ZAR
items: Quote currency: the price is in rand

groups.title: 17.9950 (bid)
items: The dealer buys dollars at this price

groups.title: 18.0050 (ask)
items: The dealer sells dollars at this price

groups.title: Spread 0.0100
items: The dealer’s margin; a round trip of US$10,000 costs R100

items.description: In the quote USD/ZAR 17.9950 / 18.0050, the dollar is the base currency and the rand the quote currency. The dealer buys dollars at 17.9950 (bid) and sells at 18.0050 (ask). The spread of 0.0100 rand is the dealer’s margin: buying and selling US$10,000 costs R100.

items.title: One-year forward USD/ZAR as rand rates change
items.description: With spot at 18.0000 and dollar rates at 4%, the one-year forward equals spot when rand rates are also 4%, and rises above spot as rand rates rise. At a 7.5% rand rate it is 18.6058.

items.title: Option profit at expiry (holder)
items.description: The call holder loses the 5 premium at any price up to 100, then gains one-for-one, breaking even at 105. The put holder loses the 4 premium at any price from 100 up, gains one-for-one below 100, and breaks even at 96. The writer’s profit is the mirror image.

items.title: How the swap fixes the borrowing cost
items.description: The company’s loan costs the reference rate plus 2%. In the swap it receives the reference rate and pays 7% fixed. The reference-rate payments cancel, leaving a fixed all-in cost of 9%. Only interest flows are exchanged; the 50 million notional never changes hands.

items.title: 10,000 over 20 years: low-cost versus high-cost fund
items.description: Two funds earn 7% a year before costs. Fund A (0.2% costs) grows 10,000 to 37,275.64 in 20 years; fund B (1.5% costs) grows it to 29,177.57. The gap of 8,098.06 is over 80% of the original investment.

items.title: The road to an IPO
items.description: The stages of an IPO taught by NYIF [S10]: preparatory and organisational meetings, due diligence, drafting the prospectus, regulatory review, investor roadshow, bookbuilding, pricing, allocation and stabilisation.

items.title: Treasury-bill auction: amount allotted by yield bid
items.description: Of 1,000 million offered, bids at 7.20% (300 million) and 7.25% (400 million) are filled in full; bids at the 7.30% clearing yield (500 million) receive 60%, or 300 million; bids at 7.35% receive nothing. Bid-to-cover is 1.4.

items.title: After the trade: the post-trade chain
items.description: After a trade is executed on trade date T, it is captured, confirmed and affirmed; cleared by a central counterparty, which becomes counterparty to both sides (novation), nets obligations and collects margin; settled at the central securities depository with delivery versus payment; and then held in custody, with income and corporate actions processed.

items.title: Shares that must move: without and with a CCP
items.description: Three trades between brokers A, B and C add up to 2,400 shares. After the CCP nets each broker’s buys and sells, only 400 shares move: an 83% reduction.

items.title: Price–yield curve: 5-year, 8% annual coupon bond
items.description: The bond’s price falls as the yield rises: 1,000 (par) when the yield equals the 8% coupon, 924.18 at 10%. The curve is convex: prices fall less when yields rise than they gain when yields fall by the same amount.

items.title: Present value of each cash flow (duration weights)
items.description: Present values at 10% of the bond’s cash flows: 72.73, 66.12, 60.11 and 54.64 for the coupons in years 1–4, and 670.60 for the final coupon plus face value in year 5. They add up to the price, 924.18. Weighting each year by its share of the price gives a Macaulay duration of 4.28 years.

items.title: Company Z: from revenue to net income (millions)
items.description: Company Z earns revenue of 1,000. After operating costs of 760 and depreciation of 40, EBIT is 200. After interest of 20, profit before tax is 180. After tax at 25% (45), net income is 135.

items.title: Where the DCF value comes from (millions)
items.description: Present values of the five forecast free cash flows are 44.25, 43.07, 41.58, 39.25 and 36.36 (204.52 in total). The present value of the terminal value is 477.29 — about 70% of the equity value of 681.81 million.

items.title: Constant-growth value as growth changes (D0 = 2.00)
items.description: Value rises steeply as growth approaches the required return. With a required return of 11%, value is 35.00 at 5% growth and 42.40 at 6%; with 12%, it is 30.00 at 5%.

items.title: One-step binomial tree
items.description: A share at 100 moves to 110 or 90. A call with strike 100 pays 10 in the up state and 0 in the down state. With a risk-free growth factor of 1.05, the risk-neutral probability of the up state is 0.75 and the call is worth (0.75 × 10) / 1.05 = 7.14 — the same as the cost of the replicating portfolio of 0.5 shares and 42.86 borrowed.

items.title: Black-Scholes-Merton values as volatility changes
items.description: With S = 100, K = 100, one year to expiry and a 5% risk-free rate, the European call is worth 10.45 at 20% volatility and becomes more valuable as volatility rises.

items.title: Portfolio risk falls as correlation falls (60% A, 40% B)
items.description: For a portfolio of 60% in asset A (standard deviation 15%) and 40% in asset B (8%), risk is 12.2% when the assets are perfectly correlated, 10.14% at a correlation of 0.2, 9.55% at zero and 5.8% at −1. Expected return stays at 8.4% throughout.

items.title: The security market line
items.description: With a 6% risk-free rate and a 12% expected market return, required return rises in a straight line with beta: 6% at beta 0, 12% at beta 1, and 15.3% at the estimated beta of 1.55. A share expected to return more than the line plots above it (positive expected alpha).

items.title: Daily returns under a normal distribution (σ = 1.2%)
items.description: A bell-shaped curve of daily returns centred on zero with a 1.2% standard deviation. 5% of days fall below −1.974% (1.645 standard deviations), which on a 10 million portfolio is the 95% one-day VaR of 197,400; 1% of days fall below −2.791% (99% VaR 279,120). VaR says nothing about how far beyond the line the worst days go.

items.title: The 20 daily returns, worst first
items.description: The 20 daily returns sorted from worst to best. The worst 10% of days are the two worst: −3.0% and −2.1%. Using the smallest loss in the tail, 90% VaR is 2.1% (21,000 on 1,000,000); expected shortfall, the average of the tail, is 2.55% (25,500).

items.title: Three stages of money laundering

nodes.label: Placement
nodes.sub: cash deposits split into small amounts

nodes.label: Layering
nodes.sub: transfers through several companies and countries

nodes.label: Integration
nodes.sub: purchase of listed shares and property

items.description: Money laundering moves through placement (cash deposits split into small amounts), layering (transfers through several companies and countries) and integration (purchase of listed shares and property). Each stage has red flags that a bank, broker or other institution should notice.

items.title: South Africa’s twin-peaks model
items.description: South Africa uses a twin-peaks model: the FSCA regulates conduct, and the Prudential Authority within the South African Reserve Bank regulates prudential soundness, alongside exchange self-regulation.

items.title: A four-step ethical decision framework
items.description: Four steps: identify the facts and stakeholders; identify duties and applicable rules; consider options and their consequences; decide, act and reflect.

items.title: The 2008 global financial crisis: a causal map

nodes.label: Reforms
nodes.sub: central clearing (M12); more bank capital and liquidity (M17)

items.description: Easy credit and rising house prices led to securitised mortgages and leverage. When house prices fell, mortgage-linked securities lost value, money-market funding ran, institutions failed or were rescued, and regulators responded with central clearing of OTC derivatives and higher bank capital and liquidity.

items.title: Developed, emerging and frontier markets

groups.title: Developed
items: Deep, liquid, open and well-regulated capital markets

groups.title: Emerging
items: Markets growing and opening, but less deep or liquid

items.description: Developed markets are high-income economies with deep, liquid, open and well-regulated capital markets. Emerging markets are middle-income economies whose capital markets are growing and opening but are less deep or liquid. Frontier markets are smaller, less liquid and less accessible, at an earlier stage of development.
